title: The butter thief
hookLine: the God who holds every world gets caught with butter on his hands, and his mother loves him anyway
carry: vatsalya: loving god like your own child
last: RAKSHA: PROTECTING YOUR PEOPLE IS DHARMA.

lines: THE SAME NIGHT, FROM THE KITCHEN.
A DAY COOKED, SUNG, STAYED UP FOR.
A HUMAN TOWER AND A POT.
cards: Same birthday, other side of the door: the kitchen. For many Hindu families, Janmashtami isn't only a story told. It's a day cooked, sung and stayed up for.
And the morning after, in Maharashtra, young men climb on each other's shoulders, level on level, to reach a clay pot of yogurt hanging over the street.

teach.h: THE CRADLE, THE CONCH, THE BATH.
teach.b: The day begins with a fast. Some take no food at all, some only fruit and milk, until midnight. A small cradle, a jhula, is set up for baby Krishna, and people sing bhajans, devotional songs.
At twelve the conch sounds, and the little image is bathed in milk and honey, dressed in tiny new clothes, and rocked.
Only then is the fast broken, often with sweets made of milk and butter. Why butter? Because of the child.
In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna grows up among cowherds in Gokul, and the women come to his mother, Yashoda, to complain: he steals our butter, he feeds it to the monkeys, he breaks the pots.
They hang the pots high; he piles up stools and mortars and climbs. Then the same chapter tells something astonishing. The boys report that Krishna has eaten dirt.
Yashoda makes him open his mouth, and inside it she sees the whole universe: sky, mountains, oceans, stars, even her own village, and herself. She's shaken.
And then, the Bhagavata says, the Lord lets her forget, and she simply picks up her boy and loves him. That's the teaching.

teach.h: VATSALYA: LOVING GOD LIKE YOUR OWN CHILD.
teach.b: Hindus call it vatsalya: loving God the way a parent loves a child. The God who holds every world chose to be scolded, fed and rocked to sleep.
It's why many families keep a small image of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, and care for him every day: bathe him, dress him, feed him.
And it's why, the day after, in Maharashtra, teams called govindas build human towers to break a pot of yogurt, Dahi Handi, cheering for the butter thief.

how: Many Hindus fast on Janmashtami, sing bhajans, bathe and dress an image of baby Krishna at midnight and rock it in a cradle, then break the fast with milk sweets; many families keep a Laddu Gopal image and care for him daily, and in Maharashtra Dahi Handi teams build human pyramids the next day.

games.q: the butter thief — tap the pairs.
p: sees the universe in his mouth
loving God like your own child

s: many families break the Janmashtami fast only after midnight
the fast ends after the image is bathed, dressed and rocked in the cradle.
Yashoda sees the whole universe inside little Krishna's mouth
then the Lord lets her forget, and she loves him as her boy.
in vatsalya, devotees keep God at a fearful distance
vatsalya is the opposite: God loved as close as your own child.

games.q: you're Yashoda. you've just seen the whole universe inside your little boy's mouth. what happens next, in the Bhagavata?
o: she bows and never treats him as a child again.
she forgets, picks him up, and loves him as her son.
she sends him away to the sages.
games.why: the Lord lets her forget, and her love as a mother goes on. that's vatsalya, the love many Hindus offer baby Krishna.

practice: Many families tend baby Krishna like a child of the house. For the sit, picture him in his cradle with butter on his hands, or a small child you love. Feel how that love asks nothing back.
On each slow breath out, say softly, Gopala, little cowherd, or if you don't pray, just rest in that tenderness. Let it be warm, not solemn.

wordCard.voice: Janmashtami. Krishna's birthday: a fast, a cradle rocked at midnight, and a God loved like a child, the butter thief.

orig.note: Hindi mākhan (butter) + cor (thief): an affectionate name for the child Krishna.

carryVoice: Your line: vatsalya, loving God like your own child. Yashoda saw the universe, then picked him up anyway. That's day six hundred seventy-seven.
